Ellicott takes the name to mean that Jah heals, places the king's birthplace in the lowland of Judah, and supposes the queen-mother was probably paramount in the government during the first years of so young a reign. Henry turns Solomon's saying both ways: woe to the land whose king is a child, but happy the land when its king is such a child. He says that being young Josiah took no bad impressions from his father's and grandfather's example but soon saw their errors, and makes the whole of it grace, the father passed by and the son a chosen vessel, grafted from the wild olive into the good, so that he fell neither into superstition nor profaneness.

Why the whole reformation is dated to the eighteenth year they answer differently. Delitzsch makes it a matter of the historian's arrangement: everything Josiah did to that end is combined into one grand picture and placed in that year because it was then that the book was discovered, through which the reformation was carried to completion, the chronological datum being repeated at the close as well as set at the head. Henry explains it instead by the resistance: Josiah began to seek the Lord much sooner, but it is to be feared the work went slowly and met with much opposition, so that he could not effect what he designed till his power was thoroughly confirmed; and he adds that time lost in our minority should quicken us afterwards, since having begun late we have need to work hard. Ellicott meets the objection that the prophetic preaching of those years is incomprehensible if idolatry had been extirpated earlier, and answers that Josiah no more than Hezekiah succeeded in rooting out the spirit of apostasy.

On the money Clarke reckons that ten years had elapsed since the offerings began, and that no one had as yet taken account of them nor applied them to the use for which they were given. Henry commends the method, a little at a time from the door-keepers, so that the burden was insensible and the contribution voluntary and not complained of; and on the clause that no reckoning was made he is of two minds, since it is to the praise of the workmen, who had gained such a reputation for honesty, but whether to the praise of those who employed them he does not know, for a man should count money after his own father.

What the book was is the chapter's first great question. Clarke asks whether this was the autograph of Moses and thinks it very probable, since the parallel account calls it the book of the law of the Lord by Moses, and supposes it the part of the fifth book containing the renewing of the covenant in the plains of Moab; he reports the rabbins' story that three idolatrous kings endeavoured to destroy all the copies, and that this one was saved by being buried under a paving-stone. Wesley says the same, the original book written by the hand of Moses and put by command beside the ark, taken thence and hid by some godly priest, and found now among the rubbish. Ellicott works from the form of the words instead: it is literally the book of the Torah that the high priest says he has found, and the definite form proves that what he found was something already known, not a book but the book of the Law. He then reports how little the critics agree, the whole Scripture, the five books, the middle three, the second and the fifth having each been proposed and each rejected; the proposal he reports with approval is a collection of Mosaic statutes afterwards worked up into the five books, set aside in the previous reign, so that after half a century of disuse it seemed new because it had been wholly forgotten.

Whether the book's contents were new to the king is disputed. Henry holds that the things contained in it were new both to him and to the high priest. Gill presses the same point, finding it strange that a king of twenty-six who had carried the reformation far should be without the book, as the high priest also was, and offers the explanation that till now they had only abstracts of the law and not the whole. Wesley takes the other side, thinking it more probable that Josiah had read it before, but that the reverence he bore the original book, and the strange and seasonable finding of it, awakened him to a more diligent consideration of it.

Why the enquiry went to Huldah rather than to Jeremiah or Zephaniah is variously answered. Ellicott says it was apparently because she dwelt in Jerusalem and they did not, Anathoth being Jeremiah's town. Henry supposes that her husband's place at court had given them longer acquaintance with her and greater assurance of her commission, and reports that the Jews say she prophesied among the court ladies, being one of them. Clarke turns it into a principle: the secret of the Lord was with neither the high priest nor the scribe nor any minister of the temple, from which we learn that a pontiff or a bishop may not possess the true knowledge of God, while a simple woman with the life of God in her soul may know more of the divine testimonies than many whose office it is to explain them. Delitzsch is more cautious: nothing further is known of her, and all we can infer is that she was highly distinguished for her prophetic gifts and that no prophet of renown was then in Jerusalem.

Two smaller points divide them. Delitzsch calls Shallum her father, where the text and the other commentators make him her husband. On the place where she lived, Ellicott rejects the rendering college as the Targum's, taken as though the word were the later name of the rabbinic collection, and holds that it means the second part of the city, the lower city; Delitzsch agrees; Wesley keeps the college and makes it where the sons of the prophets met for their teachers' instructions.

Her answer they read alike. Henry notes that she returned it not in the language of a courtier but in the dialect of a prophetess, bidding them carry word to the man that sent them, since even kings, though gods to us, are men to God; Wesley says simply that she uses no compliments. Delitzsch marks the exactness of the address, the first part of the announcement being for the man who had sent them and the second for the king of Judah, and holds that she intentionally used the general term in the first. Whether the promise of a grave in peace was kept, given that he fell at Megiddo, is the chapter's last question. Clarke argues that he was mortally wounded there but certainly not killed there, since his servants put him in his second chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died in peace; and he adds that Josiah should not have meddled in the quarrel at all, but did it in error and suffered for it, which does not impeach the prophetess. Henry refers the word not to the manner of his death but to its time, before the captivity, and adds that he died in the favour of God, which no circumstances of dying could alter. Wesley takes it of a time of public peace, since otherwise he died in battle, and of peace with God besides. Ellicott limits the promise by the clause that follows, that his eyes should not see the evil, so that he was slain in battle but spared the greater calamity of seeing his people's ruin.
